References

Public sources, every chapter

This course uses only publicly available sources. Every number, every story, every protagonist is drawn from data anyone with a browser can verify. This page lists those sources, organised by what each one is for.

The textbook this course is adapted from

Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014). Inference and Intervention: Causal Models for Business Analysis. Routledge.

The textbook this course is built on. Ryall and Bramson developed the framework — qualitative pictures, quantitative tables, decision maps, game theory, structure learning — for business decisions. We have adapted every chapter for public health and Maternal & Newborn Health, with new examples drawn entirely from public MNH data.

Causal inference and decision theory

  • Pearl, J. & Mackenzie, D. (2018). The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect. Basic Books. The most readable introduction to causal inference in print.
  • Pearl, J., Glymour, M. & Jewell, N. (2016). Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer. Wiley. Short, careful, with worked examples.
  • Hernán, M. A. & Robins, J. M. (2020). Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Open-access at hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book.
  • Spirtes, P., Glymour, C. & Scheines, R. (2000). Causation, Prediction, and Search (2nd ed.). MIT Press. The foundational text on the PC algorithm and structure learning. Open-access online.
  • Howard, R. A. & Abbas, A. E. (2015). Foundations of Decision Analysis. Pearson. The textbook on decision trees, expected value, and the value of perfect information.
  • Dixit, A. & Nalebuff, B. (2008). The Art of Strategy. Norton. The most readable introduction to game theory ever written. No equations.
  • Gigerenzer, G. (2002). Calculated Risks: How to Know When Numbers Deceive You. Simon & Schuster. The book that convinced an entire generation of doctors to teach probability in natural frequencies.
  • Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. Journal of Finance, 7(1). The classic finance paper that started portfolio thinking. Twelve pages. Worth reading once.

Maternal & Newborn Health data sources

Source What’s there Where
WHO Global Health Observatory Country-level MNH indicators who.int/data/gho
UNICEF Data Warehouse Child and maternal health indicators by country data.unicef.org
DHS Program Household-level Demographic and Health Surveys for Ethiopia, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, and many others dhsprogram.com
DHIS2 Open-source national health information system used in 70+ countries dhis2.org
Lives Saved Tool (LiST) Open-source modelling tool from Johns Hopkins for estimating lives saved by MNH interventions livessavedtool.org
World Bank Open Data Country-level economic, demographic, and health indicators data.worldbank.org

Country-specific sources used in this course

Ethiopia (Chapters 1, 5)

  • DHS Ethiopia 2000, 2005, 2011, 2016 — successive Demographic and Health Surveys
  • WHO, 2013 — Success Factors for Women’s and Children’s Health: Ethiopia
  • Wang, H. et al., 2014 — “Global, regional, and national levels of neonatal, infant, and under-5 mortality.” The Lancet, 384(9947). Open-access.
  • Federal Ministry of Health Ethiopia — Health Sector Transformation Plan II (2020/21–2024/25)
  • Tigray Regional Health Bureau, 2014 — public summary of regional health programme outputs

Rwanda (Chapter 2)

  • DHS Rwanda 2000, 2010, 2014/15, 2019/20
  • Rwanda Biomedical Centre, 2020 — Annual Health Statistics Booklet
  • Farmer, P. et al., 2013 — “Reduced premature mortality in Rwanda: lessons from success.” BMJ, 346:f65. Open-access.

Kenya (Chapters 3, 7, 9)

  • Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Schedule 4 — the legal basis for devolution to 47 counties
  • Kenya Health Information System (KHIS) — county dashboards at hiskenya.org
  • Office of the Auditor-General, Kenya — county budget execution reports at oagkenya.go.ke
  • Office of the Controller of Budget, Kenya — quarterly county budget implementation reports at cob.go.ke
  • Kenya County Public Expenditure Reviews (World Bank, 2014–2020) — open-access analyses of county-level health budgeting
  • Bourbonnais, N., 2013 — Implementing Free Maternal Health Care in Kenya: Challenges, Strategies, and Recommendations. Kenya National Commission on Human Rights.

Tanzania (Chapters 4, 10)

  • Tanzania Service Provision Assessment (TSPA) 2014/15 — facility-level survey at dhsprogram.com
  • WHO, 2017 — Trends in maternal mortality: 1990 to 2015
  • DHIS2 Tanzania — national HMIS at moh.go.tz
  • Tanzania Health Sector Strategic Plan V (2021–2026) — Ministry of Health policy document

Methodological notes used in this course

  • Simpson, E. H. (1951). “The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, B 13. The original paper on what we now call Simpson’s Paradox.
  • Pearl, J. (2014). “Comment: Understanding Simpson’s Paradox.” American Statistician, 68(1). Open-access. The clearest modern treatment.
  • Lu, C. et al., 2010. “Public financing of health in developing countries: a cross-national systematic analysis.” The Lancet, 375(9723). The classic open-access study of donor crowding-out.
  • Croicu, M. et al., 2017. Reporting bias in routine health information systems. WHO Bulletin, 95(7). Open-access.
  • Brookings Institution, 2021. Financing the SDGs: Health and Education. Open-access methodological notes on portfolio allocation in global health.

Pedagogy

  • Heath, C. & Heath, D. (2007). Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die. Random House. The pedagogical framework this course is built on — every chapter follows the SUCCES principles (Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories) deliberately.

A note on protagonists

Every named protagonist in this course — Almaz, Beatrice, Faith, Joyce, Hiwot, Hassan, Naomi, David, Grace, Wangari, Patrick, Esther — is a composite. The details (ages, locations, situations, decisions) are drawn from the public sources listed above. The names are not real. Composites are clearly labeled at every introduction. We use this convention to give each chapter an emotional anchor without putting any real person on the spot.
